title: Three perfect days in San Francisco, from Telegraph Hill to the Golden Gate
dek: Beat-era North Beach on Friday, a Día de los Muertos concert at Davies Symphony Hall on Saturday, and on Sunday a coffee festival at Fort Mason and a walk along the bay to the Golden Gate Bridge.

hero.caption: The Golden Gate Bridge, where Sunday's walk along Crissy Field ends as the light goes.

intro:
The first weekend after the clocks go back is a quieter one in San Francisco. Halloween in the Castro is over, the holiday lights are only starting to go up, and the sun sets around 5 p.m., so the best views come in the afternoon and the evenings belong to bars, dinners and concerts.

There is still plenty on. On Saturday afternoon the **San Francisco Symphony** plays its annual Día de los Muertos concert at Davies Symphony Hall, with music by Carlos Chávez, Arturo Márquez and José Pablo Moncayo, a world premiere by Luis Farfán Carrillo, and altars and art in the lobby. The 10th **San Francisco Coffee Festival** fills the Festival Pavilion at Fort Mason on Saturday and Sunday. At the zoo, **ZooLights** opens on Friday with more than a million lights, and the Warriors play the Orlando Magic at Chase Center on Saturday evening. On Sunday morning the **Veterans Day Parade** runs along the Embarcadero and Jefferson Street at Fisherman's Wharf, ahead of the holiday itself on Wednesday.

The plan keeps each day to one part of town. Friday is North Beach and Chinatown: focaccia, Coit Tower, City Lights and a Beat bar. Saturday is Hayes Valley and the Civic Center, with the Asian Art Museum, the Painted Ladies and the symphony. Sunday heads to the northern waterfront, from Fort Mason past the Marina and Crissy Field to the Mess Hall, the new food hall at Presidio Tunnel Tops, and out onto the bridge before dark.

days.title: Friday: North Beach, Telegraph Hill and Chinatown
days.intro: The old Italian quarter and the Beat writers' haunts, with a climb to Coit Tower and an afternoon in Chinatown next door.

stops.name: Liguria Bakery
stops.text: Start at the corner of Washington Square with focaccia from this old North Beach bakery, which makes little else. Order it plain, with rosemary, or as a pizza focaccia, wrapped in paper to eat on a bench in the square across the street, with the twin spires of Saints Peter and Paul Church above you. Go early: Liguria closes at noon and often sells out well before then, so the later you arrive, the fewer flavors are left.

stops.name: Coit Tower
stops.text: Walk up Filbert Street from Washington Square to the top of Telegraph Hill. Inside the tower's base, 27 fresco murals painted during the Great Depression by local artists show daily life in San Francisco, including the struggles of working people; the ground floor is free. The elevator to the observation deck costs $8 for visitors and gives a full circle of views over the bay, the bridges and downtown. From November the tower is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The hill is steep from every side, so wear good shoes.

stops.name: City Lights Bookstore
stops.text: Lawrence Ferlinghetti co-founded City Lights in 1953, and in 1956 he published Allen Ginsberg's *Howl*, then fought the obscenity charges that followed. The shop is still independent, with a deep stock of new and used fiction, poetry and politics. Browse the floors, then cross Jack Kerouac Alley, the lane beside the store, to see where you will end the evening. Gioia Woods, who wrote a new history of the shop, calls it a "cultural first responder" for the way it takes up each decade's fights.

stops.name: Golden Boy Pizza
stops.text: Lunch is a square slice or two at this Green Street institution. The Sicilian-style pizza has a thick, crisp-edged crust; get pepperoni, sausage, or the clam and garlic, the one to try if you only have room for one. Slices are about $4 each, so this is the cheapest good meal of the weekend. Take your slices back to Washington Square if the sun is out, and save room for a cannoli at Stella Pastry on Columbus.

stops.name: Grant Avenue and Chinatown
stops.text: From Green Street, walk south along Grant Avenue into Chinatown. Duck into the side alleys, look up at the painted balconies, and stop at the bakeries and tea shops as they catch your eye. Stockton Street, a block west, is where the neighborhood does its own shopping for produce, fish and roast meats. Finish at the Dragon Gate at Bush Street, then walk back up Grant toward North Beach as the light goes, around 5 p.m.

stops.name: Red Window
stops.text: A Spanish-leaning tapas bar on the corner of Columbus and Green, open from 4 p.m. on Fridays. Order at least two plates of patatas bravas, along with croquetas, jamón and something from the cocktail list; diners this fall also praise the braised short rib and the mussels and clams. Book a table on OpenTable, or try for a seat at the bar if you come early.

stops.name: Vesuvio Cafe
stops.text: End the night across Jack Kerouac Alley from City Lights, in the bar where Kerouac, Ginsberg and Ferlinghetti drank. Vesuvio has been pouring since 1948, and its two floors are crowded with murals, Tiffany lamps and decades of photos and odd objects. Take a seat upstairs by the front window, order a martini, and watch Columbus Avenue. It's open until 2 a.m. on Fridays and serves no food, and there are no reservations, so arrive hungry for nothing but conversation.

days.title: Saturday: Hayes Valley, the Civic Center and the symphony
days.intro: Pastries, a great museum of Asian art, the Painted Ladies, and the symphony's Día de los Muertos concert, all within a short walk of one another.

stops.name: Loquat
stops.text: Breakfast is at this bakery and cafe on Gough Street, which opens at 8 a.m. The cases lean toward Jewish baking: get a mini chocolate babka, a seasonal boureka and a coffee, and a chocolate chip cookie for later. It's a small room, so on a fine morning take your order to Patricia's Green, the park a few blocks west on Hayes Street, before you walk to the museum.

stops.name: Asian Art Museum
stops.text: The museum fills the city's former main library across from City Hall, and its collection spans thousands of years of art from across the continent. Give it two hours, and check the special exhibitions page before you go. It opens at 10 a.m. Friday through Monday and is closed on Tuesday and Wednesday, so Saturday morning works well. Reserve a ticket online ahead of time.

stops.name: Dumpling Home
stops.text: Walk back to Gough Street for lunch at this small dumpling shop. Order the shengjianbao, the pan-fried pork buns with crisp bottoms and hot soup inside, plus a basket of xiao long bao and a green onion pancake to share. It takes no reservations and a line forms at the door at lunch on weekends, but it moves, and the dumplings come quickly once you are seated.

stops.name: Alamo Square and the Painted Ladies
stops.text: Walk west up Hayes Street for about 15 minutes to Alamo Square. The park climbs to a hilltop with a view east over downtown, framed by the row of Victorian houses on Steiner Street known as the Painted Ladies. It's the city's most photographed postcard and still worth the climb. Find a spot on the grass, then head back down Hayes Street with time to reach Davies Symphony Hall before 3 p.m.

stops.name: San Francisco Symphony: Día de los Muertos
stops.text: The symphony's yearly celebration of the Day of the Dead, with José Luis Gómez conducting, violinist Francisco Fullana, two salterio players, and Casa Círculo Cultural. The program has music by Carlos Chávez, Arturo Márquez and José Pablo Moncayo and a new piece commissioned from Luis Farfán Carrillo. Come early to see the altars and art by local artists in the lobby. Tickets start at $34.50, and children's seats are half price.

stops.name: Rich Table
stops.text: Dinner is a short walk from the hall at one of the city's best-loved restaurants. Start with the dried porcini doughnuts and the sardine chips, two snacks that have been on the menu for years, then the aged beef wonton with chili crunch and the plancha fried rice for the table. Tables open on Resy 45 days ahead at midnight and go quickly, but the bar holds seats for walk-ins every day, so arrive at opening if you have no booking.

days.title: Sunday: Fort Mason, Crissy Field and the Golden Gate
days.intro: A coffee festival on the water, then a flat walk along the bay to lunch at the Presidio and the bridge at dusk.

stops.name: San Francisco Coffee Festival
stops.text: The 10th festival fills the Festival Pavilion on the bay with Bay Area roasters and other exhibitors. Tickets start at $29 and include unlimited tastings, so pace yourself: talk to the roasters at their booths, catch a panel, and buy beans to take home. There is live music too. Saturday's hours are 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; check the festival site for Sunday's before you go, and eat something first.

stops.name: Marina Green to Crissy Field
stops.text: From Fort Mason, follow the bay west along the Marina Green, past the yacht harbor, to Crissy Field, a restored tidal marsh and beach with the Golden Gate Bridge in front of you the whole way. It's flat, easy walking and the best way to see the bridge grow. The Palace of Fine Arts is a short detour south through the Marina if you want it. Bring a layer: the wind off the Golden Gate picks up in the afternoon.

stops.name: The Mess Hall
stops.text: The Presidio's new food hall opened in August in an 1897 building moved within Tunnel Tops park, with its original wood floors and long views of the bridge, Alcatraz and the Palace of Fine Arts. Three counters share one kitchen: Boda for Korean fried chicken and mandu, Day Boat for oysters, chowder and hand rolls, and Breadwinner for subs and smashburgers. There's a full bar with local beer. Restaurant menus start at 11 a.m., and most seats face the water.

stops.name: Golden Gate Bridge
stops.text: From Tunnel Tops, follow the bay trail west along Crissy Field to the south end of the bridge, then walk out over the strait for as long as you like. Out in the middle the city, Alcatraz and the Marin Headlands are all in view, and the wind and the noise of the traffic are part of it. Sunset is around 5 p.m., so turn back by 4:30 to be off the span while the light is still good. A rideshare from the bridge back to the Marina is a short trip.

stops.name: A16
stops.text: End the weekend on Chestnut Street at this long-running southern Italian restaurant, which still fills up on Sunday nights. The Neapolitan pizzas are the most ordered dishes, the margherita and the marinara in particular, and the arugula salad with apple, ricotta salata and hazelnuts is a good start. It serves from noon to 9:30 p.m. on Sundays. Book on OpenTable.

stay.name: Four Seasons Hotel San Francisco at Embarcadero
stay.text: The hotel takes the upper floors of a downtown tower near Jackson Square and the Transamerica Pyramid, so the rooms look out over the skyline, the bay and the Golden Gate Bridge. In October it kept its two Michelin Keys for a third year, and its restaurant, Orafo, is worth a dinner of its own. North Beach is a short walk, which puts Friday's plan close by.

stay.name: Fairmont San Francisco
stay.text: The grand old hotel on top of Nob Hill, where delegates drafted the United Nations Charter in 1945. Have a drink in the Tonga Room, a tiki bar built over the old indoor pool, where a rainstorm rolls across the lagoon every half hour. The Powell-Hyde and Powell-Mason cable cars and the 1 California bus reach the hotel, and North Beach and Chinatown are downhill on foot.

stay.name: Hotel Bohème
stay.text: A small hotel of 15 rooms on Columbus Avenue, decorated for Beat-era North Beach, with black-and-white photos from the 1950s and one room named for Allen Ginsberg. Rooms are small, but you are steps from City Lights, Vesuvio and Red Window, which makes it the right base for Friday. Don't bring a car.

events.name: Warriors vs. Miami Heat
events.text: If you arrive Thursday, the Warriors open a run of three home games in five nights against the Heat.

events.name: ZooLights opening weekend
events.text: More than a million lights across 14 zones, from a butterfly pathway to a lit Golden Gate Bridge and cable car, opening Friday and running to January 3. Tickets are $30 for adults and $21 for children, separate from day admission; closed Mondays and Tuesdays until December 16.

events.name: San Francisco Coffee Festival
events.when: Sat. 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and Sun.
events.text: The 10th festival brings Bay Area roasters, tastings, panels and live music to the waterfront for two days. Tickets start at $29.

events.name: San Francisco Symphony: Día de los Muertos
events.where: Davies Symphony Hall, 201 Van Ness Ave
events.text: José Luis Gómez conducts music by Chávez, Márquez and Moncayo and a world premiere, with lobby installations by local artists. From $34.50; children half price.

events.name: Warriors vs. Orlando Magic
events.text: A Saturday evening home game; it clashes with dinner in Hayes Valley, so pick one or the other.

events.name: Veterans Day Parade
events.where: The Embarcadero and Jefferson St., Fisherman's Wharf
events.text: The parade forms on North Point and runs north on the Embarcadero, then along Jefferson Street to Aquatic Park, ahead of Veterans Day on Wednesday, November 11.

events.name: Blankets & Blockbusters: Toy Story 5
events.text: A free outdoor screening on the plaza beside Chase Center. Bring a blanket; seating is first come, first served.

know: **From the airport.** From SFO, BART takes about 30 minutes to Powell Street on a weekday and 40 to 45 minutes late at night and on weekends; the fare is a little over $10, and you can tap a contactless card at the gate. A taxi takes about 30 minutes and costs roughly $45 to $60 on the meter.

**Getting around.** A Muni 1-Day Visitor Passport costs $15 and covers buses, Muni Metro, the historic streetcars and the cable cars, but not BART. Buy it on MuniMobile, at kiosks or on a Clipper card; Clipper and tap-to-pay also work everywhere.

**Sunday's parade.** From 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Sunday, the Embarcadero north of North Point, Jefferson Street and the streets north of Beach between Hyde and the Embarcadero are closed for the Veterans Day Parade. From 8:30 a.m. to 3 p.m., F line streetcars turn back at the Ferry Building, with shuttle buses to Fisherman's Wharf, and the 8, 28 and 39 buses end short of the Wharf.
**Short days.** Clocks went back on November 1, and the sun now sets around 5 p.m. Do Coit Tower and the bridge in daylight, and bring a warm layer for the wind on the waterfront.
**Closed days.** The Asian Art Museum is closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays, and ZooLights is dark Mondays and Tuesdays until mid-December; neither affects this weekend.

**Tipping.** California law requires restaurants to show any service charge or surcharge on the menu. Read the bill before you tip so you don't pay twice; otherwise tip as you would anywhere in the US.
